blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning-critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL-based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph--reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time-indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout-return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8\%, 60.8\%, and 27.4\%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4\%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID-Planner.

blocks.en: 1. Introduction
blocks.zh: 1. 联合国 导言

blocks.en: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting ego trajectories that are safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions ( Caesar et al., 2021 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Dauner et al., 2023 ; Jia et al., 2023a ; Jia et al., 2024 ) . Despite rapid progress in learning-based planning, robust closed-loop decision making in dense urban scenes remains challenging ( Caesar et al., 2021 ; Dauner et al., 2023 ; Jia et al., 2024 ) . A core challenge is that planning performance depends not only on average-case trajectory realism but on learning from a small set of planning-critical trajectories—those arising in highly interactive, safety-sensitive, and rule-constrained scenarios such as merging, yielding, and intersection conflicts ( Caesar et al., 2021 ; Dauner et al., 2023 ; Jia et al., 2024 ) . In practice, however, most training trajectories are semantically flat, weakly constrained, and low-conflict, contributing limited signals to the decision boundaries that matter most for planning ( Dauner et al., 2023 ) . This long-tail structure makes pure imitation learning insufficient, since abundant easy trajectories dominate supervision, while naive reinforcement learning is also inadequate because generic rewards are difficult to design stably for complex multi-agent interactions. These challenges motivate graph-structured relational modeling to prioritize planning-critical trajectories and support planning-oriented policy improvement.
blocks.zh: 自主驾驶规划需要选择在复杂的多剂相互作用下安全,符合规则,舒适的自负轨迹(Caesar等,2021;Hu等,2023;Dauner等,2023;Jia等,2023a;Jia等,2024). 尽管在以学习为基础的规划方面取得迅速进展,但在密集的城市场景中,强有力的封闭式决策仍然具有挑战性(Caesar等,2021;Dauner等,2023;Jia等,2024)。 一项核心挑战是,规划业绩不仅取决于平均轨迹的现实主义,而且取决于学习一小套规划关键轨迹——这些轨迹产生于高度互动、安全敏感和规则限制的情景,例如合并、产生和交叉冲突(Caesar等,2021;Dauner等,2023;Jia等,2024)。 然而,实际上,大多数培训轨迹都非常平坦,受限程度低,冲突程度低,对规划中最重要的决定界限的信号有限(Dauner等,2023年)。 这种长尾结构使得纯模仿学习不足,因为丰富的容易的轨迹主导了监督,而天真强化学习也不够充分,因为通用奖励很难为复杂的多剂相互作用而被精确地设计出. 这些挑战促使采用图表结构关系模型,确定规划关键轨迹的优先次序,支持以规划为导向的政策改进。

blocks.en: Existing methods improve planning from different angles, but the core issue remains unresolved. Strong imitation-based planners, such as UrbanDriver ( Scheel et al., 2022 ) , PlanTF ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , and PLUTO ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) , optimize similarity to expert behavior, allowing abundant easy trajectories to dominate training and under-emphasizing safety-critical and rule-sensitive cases. Interaction-centric methods, such as GameFormer ( Huang et al., 2023b ) , improve multi-agent relation modeling, but mainly at the representation level, without explicitly using relational structure to determine trajectory value or optimization priority. Diffusion-based planners, such as Diffusion Planner ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , provide flexible multi-modal trajectory generation, while reward-guided variants such as Diffusion-ES ( Yang et al., 2024 ) demonstrate the promise of reward-driven optimization. However, existing approaches still rely either on behavior cloning objectives, which suffer from compounding errors and exposure bias in closed-loop inference, or on generic reward-driven optimization, which does not explicitly encode planning-oriented relational semantics. This leaves open how relational semantics should shape both the training distribution and the optimization objective, rather than serving only as scene representations or sampling-time guidance.
blocks.zh: 现有方法从不同角度改进了规划,但核心问题仍未得到解决。 以模仿为主的强力规划者,如"UrbanDriver"(Scheel等,2022年),"PlanTF"(Cheng等,2023年)和"PLUTO"(Cheng等,2024年),优化了与专家行为的相似性,使得丰富的轻松出行的轨迹能够主导培训,对安全批评和规则敏感度不高的案件不够强调. 以互动为中心的方法,如GameFormer(Huang等,2023年b),改进了多代理关系模型,但主要是在代表级别,没有明确使用关系结构来确定轨迹值或优化优先级. 以传播为主的规划者,如传播计划者(郑等,2025年)提供灵活的多模式轨迹生成,而奖励制导的变体如传播-ES(杨等,2024年)则显示出奖励驱动优化的希望. 然而,现有的方法仍然依赖于行为克隆目标,后者在闭路推论中存在复合错误和曝光偏差;或者依赖于通用的奖励驱动优化,后者没有明确编码规划导向的关系语义. 这使得关系语义应如何塑造训练分布和优化目标,而不是仅仅作为场景表现或取样时间指导。

blocks.en: To address this gap, we propose GRID-Planner , a G raph- R eward I ntegrated D iffusion planner that uses graph-structured scene semantics to directly shape the optimization signal of generative planning. Rather than treating graph structure as just an input representation, we use it to define both trajectory importance and planning-oriented return. Our framework answers three questions left open by prior planners: which trajectories should matter more during training, how their quality should be evaluated for planning, and how relational signals should reshape diffusion-based policy learning. Specifically, our framework contains three tightly coupled components: ❶ Graph-Aware Importance Weighting , which upweights trajectories from complex, high-risk scenes using scene-interaction centrality and collision-risk cues; ❷ Relational Reward Surrogate (RRS), which evaluates candidate rollouts through time-indexed ego-centric scene graphs, producing a dense trajectory-level signal with smooth bounded penalties over safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort; and ❸ Graph-Reward Integrated Diffusion Objective , which incorporates structured returns into a low-variance advantage-weighted diffusion objective, coupled with an advantage-gated on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mechanism. The resulting advantage reweights diffusion denoising and gates OPSD teacher selection and updates, forming a rollout–return–advantage–update loop in which graph-reward signals directly drive policy improvement.

blocks.en: The main contributions of this work are: • We propose GRID-Planner , a unified graph-reward integrated diffusion framework that redefines how scene graphs are used in autonomous driving planning: rather than serving only as input representations, they directly shape optimization priority and trajectory value for closed-loop decision making. • We introduce a planning-oriented relational learning mechanism , instantiated by Graph-Aware Importance Weighting and a Relational Reward Surrogate , which together focus training on planning-critical trajectories and score candidate rollouts using safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort criteria. • We develop a unified on-policy diffusion objective that combines advantage-weighted diffusion with advantage-gated self-distillation to support stable on-policy refinement and consolidate high-return behaviors, yielding consistent gains over strong baselines on nuPlan and interPlan.

blocks.en: 2. Related Work
blocks.zh: 2. 相关工作

blocks.en:
Imitation-Based and Interaction-Centric Planning. A major line of work learns autonomous driving policies from expert demonstrations ( Caesar et al., 2021 ; Dauner et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Prakash et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Jia et al., 2023b ; Jia et al., 2023a ) . UrbanDriver ( Scheel et al., 2022 ) , PlanTF ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) , and PLUTO ( Cheng et al., 2024 ) achieve strong closed-loop performance through carefully designed imitation objectives, while UniAD ( Hu et al., 2023 ) , VAD ( Jiang et al., 2023a ) ,
VADv2 ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , SparseDrive ( Sun et al., 2024 ) ,
DTPP ( Huang et al., 2023a ) , GameFormer ( Huang et al., 2023b ) ,
InterFuser ( Shao et al., 2023 ) , and Causal-Planner ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) improve scene representation and interaction modeling. However, these approaches mainly optimize expert imitation or relational representations, without explicitly using scene relations to determine trajectory importance or planner-oriented value. GRID-Planner instead uses graph structure to prioritize planning-critical trajectories and construct relational returns over safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort.

blocks.en: Generative Planning with Diffusion. Generative planners model future trajectories as samples from expressive distributions, supporting multi-modal driving behaviors ( Jiang et al., 2023b ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . GenAD ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) , Diffusion Planner ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and Diffusion-ES ( Yang et al., 2024 ) explore latent generation, diffusion-based closed-loop planning, and reward-guided sampling, respectively. Flow Planner ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , DiffusionDrive ( Liao et al., 2025 ) , and BridgeDrive ( Liu et al., 2026 ) further improve interactive modeling and diffusion-policy design. These methods primarily focus on trajectory generation or sampling-time guidance, whereas GRID-Planner incorporates structured relational signals into training through trajectory prioritization, relational evaluation, and diffusion-policy refinement.

blocks.en: RL-Based Policy Improvement for Generative Planning. Reinforcement learning has been combined with diffusion policies for reward-driven optimization. DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) , advantage-weighted regression methods ( Peng et al., 2019 ; Nair et al., 2021 ) , and diffusion policies ( Wang et al., 2023 ) adapt policy-improvement principles to expressive generative models. However, they generally rely on generic scalar rewards rather than planning-oriented relational semantics. GRID-Planner couples graph-weighted relational returns with advantage-weighted denoising and advantage-gated on-policy self-distillation, allowing relational signals to directly shape policy updates.

blocks.en: 3.2. Problem Statement
blocks.zh: 3.2. 问题说明

blocks.en:
At each planning step, we represent the driving scene as a relational graph G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) , where nodes V V include the ego vehicle, surrounding agents, lane polylines, and traffic signals, and edges E E encode geometric relations and traffic-rule priorities.
We consider trajectory planning over a candidate trajectory τ \tau and define the trajectory-level relational score (3) ℛ RRS ​ ( τ ) = R safety ​ ( τ ) + R rule ​ ( τ ) + R comfort ​ ( τ ) , \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{RRS}}(\tau)=R_{\mathrm{safety}}(\tau)+R_{\mathrm{rule}}(\tau)+R_{\mathrm{comfort}}(\tau), which evaluates safety, rule compliance, and ride comfort (each term is specified in the next subsection).

To align this trajectory-level evaluator with entropy-regularized distribution shaping, we use a trajectory return surrogate: (4) R traj ​ ( τ ) = w ⁡ ( τ ) ​ ℛ RRS ​ ( τ ) , R_{\mathrm{traj}}(\tau)=w(\tau)\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{RRS}}(\tau), where w ⁡ ( τ ) ≥ 0 w(\tau)\geq 0 is an importance weight used to differentiate candidate rollouts. Our goal is to learn a graph-conditioned trajectory distribution π θ ​ ( τ | G ) \pi_{\theta}(\tau|G) that concentrates probability mass on trajectories with higher R traj ​ ( τ ) R_{\mathrm{traj}}(\tau) , while maintaining diversity and efficient inference. To achieve this, we employ a unified graph-reward integrated diffusion objective (Sec. 3.5 ), which combines advantage-weighted diffusion updates with a state-value baseline and on-policy self-distillation, aligning training with planner-induced rollouts and consolidating high-reward behaviors, as illustrated in Fig. 2 .

The “graph” here is a lightweight scene-interaction proxy used only
for weighting (distinct from the model conditioning graph), as illustrated in
Fig. 3 .

blocks.en: nuPlan and interPlan Datasets. We evaluate GRID-Planner in closed-loop simulation on two established autonomous driving benchmarks. Following the standard protocol ( Cheng et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) , we report nuPlan ( Caesar et al., 2021 ) results on Val14 , Test14-random , and Test14-hard , covering general performance and long-tail robustness. We further evaluate on interPlan ( Hallgarten et al., 2024 ) , which emphasizes interaction-intensive scenarios such as nudging around parked vehicles, unprotected overtaking, and jaywalker encounters.

blocks.en: 4.2. Implementation Details
blocks.zh: 4.2. 实施细节

blocks.en: GRID-Planner uses 2 seconds of history to predict an 8-second trajectory at 10 Hz, with 21 historical timestamps including the current frame and 80 future steps. Each waypoint is represented as ( x , y , cos ⁡ θ , sin ⁡ θ ) (x,y,\cos\theta,\sin\theta) in the ego-centric frame. The scene encoder retains up to 32 neighboring agents, 70 lane polylines, 25 route-lane polylines, and 5 static control elements. Training has three stages: (1) base diffusion training for 400 epochs with AdamW (batch size 2048, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.01, and EMA decay 0.999), CFG, and 0.3 neighbor dropout; (2) graph-aware reward fine-tuning with GAIW and RRS for 10 epochs at 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} ; and (3) online self-distillation for 2 epochs, sampling four candidates per scene and ranking their graph-weighted returns to select the teacher and supervise the student. At inference, the distilled planner uses four update steps with a CFG scale of 1.8. Latency is the mean planner-side compute_trajectory runtime at batch size 1 on the same hardware, excluding simulator overhead, and is reported only as a relative runtime diagnostic.

blocks.en: 4.3. Main Results
blocks.zh: 4.3. 主要成果

blocks.en: nuPlan benchmark. Table 1 reports closed-loop planning results on nuPlan under both non-reactive (NR) and reactive (R) protocols. Among learning-based planners, GRID-Planner achieves the best performance on five of the six splits. Compared with the strong Flow Planner baseline (reproduced locally using its official open-source implementation 1 1 1 https://github.com/DiffusionAD/Flow-Planner ), our method improves Val14-R from 79.90 to 82.59 and, more importantly, raises the highly challenging Test14-hard-R score from 66.88 to 71.15, an absolute gain of +4.27. The gains are consistently larger on reactive and hard splits, indicating that GRID-Planner is particularly effective in planning-critical settings, where success depends on resolving dense interactions rather than merely generating plausible nominal trajectories. Similar trends also hold on the non-reactive splits, suggesting that the proposed training strategy improves not only interaction robustness but also overall closed-loop planning quality.

blocks.en: interPlan benchmark. Table 2 further evaluates interactive decision making on interPlan, which emphasizes long-tail interactive scenarios beyond standard lane following. GRID-Planner achieves the best overall score of 57.25, outperforming both Diffusion Planner and Flow Planner (52.90 and 54.83, respectively). The improvement is especially evident in spatially constrained and highly uncertain scenarios, including High Traffic Density (65.37 vs. 56.41 against Flow Planner) and Jaywalk (43.20 vs. 41.64 against Flow Planner, and 26.20 against Diffusion Planner). Since success in these categories depends on resolving ambiguous right-of-way conflicts rather than nominal path tracking, these results support the role of the proposed relational learning mechanism in shaping safer and more interaction-aware behavior. The gains are not uniform across all categories: in Nudge Around , GRID-Planner slightly exceeds Flow Planner (58.77 vs. 58.02) but remains below Diffusion Planner (60.48), suggesting that our method is most advantageous in scenarios where relational reasoning and safety–progress trade-offs under dynamic uncertainty dominate the planning difficulty. Qualitative rollouts in Fig. 5 further support this observation: in several challenging intersection scenarios, the baseline collides while GRID-Planner remains safe on the same scenes, showing improved closed-loop handling of interactive conflicts.

blocks.en: Main ablation. Table 3 shows that the major components of GRID-Planner provide complementary gains. Starting from the pure diffusion baseline, progressively introducing graph-aware weighting, relational return shaping, and on-policy optimization steadily improves the official score from 79.90 to 82.59 . Specifically, adding GAIW raises the score to 80.92 while reducing collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk, indicating that prioritizing planning-critical scenes already strengthens the effective training signal. Adding the graph-weighted trajectory return R traj R_{\mathrm{traj}} further improves the score to 81.31 and yields the strongest comfort and lane-keeping performance at this stage, suggesting better alignment with planning-oriented safety and rule constraints. Building on this, on-policy actor–critic optimization increases the score to 81.92 and substantially reduces collisions, although jerk slightly increases, indicating a temporary comfort–safety trade-off during rollout-based policy improvement. Adding OPSD partially recovers comfort and efficiency while preserving the score gain. The full model achieves the best overall score together with the lowest lane deviation and latency, while maintaining near-best safety and comfort metrics. Overall, these results support the intended role of each component: GAIW emphasizes planning-critical trajectories, R traj R_{\mathrm{traj}} injects dense relational planning signals, and the on-policy objective with OPSD consolidates these signals into a stronger closed-loop planner.

blocks.en: Ablating the graph-aware weighting mechanism. Table 4 and Fig. 6 validate both the effectiveness of GAIW and the necessity of its stabilization design. Compared with no weighting ( w ⁡ ( τ ) = 1 w(\tau)=1 ), using either graph centrality or collision-risk weighting alone already improves the score (81.74/81.82 vs. 81.61) while reducing collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk, showing that both structural complexity and explicit risk cues help prioritize planning-critical trajectories. Among the single-factor variants, risk-only weighting yields slightly better score and safety metrics than centrality-only , whereas centrality-only achieves slightly lower jerk, suggesting that the two cues capture complementary aspects of planning difficulty. When both cues are combined, stabilization becomes crucial: removing either w w -clipping or mean-normalization degrades performance, while Full + stabilization achieves the best overall result, with the highest score ( 82.07 ) and the lowest collision rate ( 0.0519 ), lane deviation ( 0.0154 ), and jerk ( 0.1252 ). This trend is consistent with Fig. 6 , where the stabilized variant maintains higher reactive closed-loop score and lower collision rate throughout training than variants without clipping or normalization, indicating improved optimization stability. Latency remains nearly unchanged across all variants, showing that the gain comes from better training signals rather than additional inference cost. Overall, these results support our design intuition: centrality emphasizes structurally complex scenes, collision-risk weighting highlights immediate safety-critical interactions, and clipping plus mean-normalization prevents overly heavy-tailed importance weights from destabilizing optimization.

blocks.en: Ablating the relational reward surrogate (RRS). Table 5 shows that the three components of RRS play distinct yet complementary roles, and that the full surrogate yields the best overall planning behavior. Using the complete reward under the full training pipeline, the planner achieves the highest score ( 82.59 ) together with the best collision rate ( 0.0503 ), lane deviation ( 0.0105 ), and jerk ( 0.1166 ), confirming that jointly modeling safety, rule consistency, and comfort is necessary for balanced closed-loop performance. Removing the rule term substantially degrades lane deviation (from 0.0105 to 0.0150) and lowers the overall score, showing that explicit rule-aware shaping is important for route-consistent behavior. Removing the comfort term leaves safety-related metrics relatively stable but worsens jerk (0.1538 vs. 0.1166) and increases latency, indicating that the comfort term is important for motion smoothness. The largest degradation occurs when removing the safety term: the score drops markedly to 74.85, while collision rate and lane deviation worsen to 0.0708 and 0.0287, respectively, demonstrating that safety remains the dominant constraint in closed-loop planning. The single-term variants further support this decomposition: safety only preserves relatively better collision performance, rule only better preserves lane consistency, and comfort only achieves the smoothest trajectories with the lowest jerk but performs poorly on overall planning quality and safety. Overall, these results match the intended design of RRS: the safety term anchors collision avoidance, the rule term enforces scene-consistent behavioral constraints, and the comfort term regularizes motion smoothness; only their combination provides a dense and well-balanced planning signal aligned with the full closed-loop objective.

blocks.en: Ablating the graph-reward integrated objective. Table 6 and Fig. 7 show that the full on-policy objective is essential for achieving the best overall closed-loop performance. Compared with offline diffusion only, the unified objective improves the score from 79.90 to 82.59 , while substantially reducing collision rate (0.0783 → \rightarrow 0.0503 ), lane deviation (0.0268 → \rightarrow 0.0105 ), and jerk (0.1606 → \rightarrow 0.1166 ), suggesting that graph-reward shaping is most effective when coupled with on-policy optimization rather than used as a purely offline surrogate. Removing the critic baseline yields only marginal gain over the offline baseline (80.03 vs. 79.90), indicating that value estimation is important for producing a usable low-variance improvement signal. Removing advantage reweighting or the OPSD term also degrades performance, with score dropping to 80.76 and 80.29, respectively, together with worse safety and tracking metrics, showing that reweighting helps focus learning on better rollouts while OPSD helps consolidate these improvements into the policy. The OPSD-specific ablations further clarify this effect: removing the advantage gate preserves relatively competitive collision, lane, jerk, and latency metrics, but still lowers the score to 80.89, suggesting that ungated distillation weakens overall policy improvement; using a random teacher causes the largest degradation (79.57 score, 0.0894 collision rate, 0.1753 jerk), demonstrating that teacher quality is crucial for successful consolidation. This trend is also reflected in Fig. 7 , where the full objective exhibits faster convergence and consistently lower collision rate during training. Overall, the results support the intended role of each component: the critic baseline stabilizes advantage estimation, advantage reweighting emphasizes better trajectories, and OPSD transfers these gains into a stronger closed-loop planner.

blocks.en: 5. Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 (韩语). 结论

blocks.en: We presented GRID-Planner , a graph–reward integrated diffusion planner that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals for autonomous driving. By combining Graph-Aware Importance Weighting (GAIW), a Relational Reward Surrogate (RRS), and a unified on-policy diffusion objective with actor–critic and self-distillation, our framework improves trajectory prioritization, rollout evaluation, and policy refinement in a coherent manner. Limitations and Future Work. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that GRID-Planner consistently improves closed-loop performance, especially in reactive and interaction-intensive scenarios, while our current design still relies on hand-crafted graph weighting and a limited set of relational reward signals; future work will explore richer relational cues, more adaptive graph-based weighting, and more efficient on-policy optimization for large-scale real-world autonomous driving deployment.
